about.p: This course prepares you for IELTS General Training, with practice in all four skills. Listening recordings are read aloud by British voices – listen first, then answer, and read the script afterwards. Reading units have a passage with exam-style questions; while you answer, you can open the passage again.

In the writing units you get the task, advice and a timer. Write your answer, compare it with the Band 9 model, and ask for feedback to get an estimated band and tips. Speaking units have questions or a cue card, timers and a recorder, so you can listen to yourself.
The vocabulary and grammar units cover the language that lifts a score from Band 6 to Band 7 and beyond.

Many of the listening scripts, writing tasks and model answers, speaking questions and topic word lists are adapted from *IELTS Materials* by Pradeep Kumar (github.com/learning-zone/ielts-materials), used under the MIT licence – see ielts-materials-LICENSE.txt. The reading passages, the exercises and the explanations were written for this course.

L.p: This course prepares you for the General Training test. Listening and Speaking are the same for General Training and Academic; Reading and Writing are different.

Each skill gets a band from 0 to 9, in half bands. Your overall band is the average of the four, rounded to the nearest half band. In Listening and Reading, band 9 needs about 39 or 40 correct answers out of 40.

L.h: C How Writing and Speaking are marked

t: every part of the task answered, with relevant, well-developed ideas
clear paragraphs and natural, varied linking
a wide, precise and accurate range of vocabulary
a variety of structures with very few errors

L.p: Speaking is marked on fluency and coherence, lexical resource, grammatical range and accuracy, and pronunciation. Each criterion counts equally.

L.tip: Because the criteria count equally, excellent vocabulary cannot make up for a task you haven't fully answered.

script: Welcome to the Riverside Local History Museum. Please ensure your audio guide is set to channel two. You may pause and replay any section at any time.

As you enter through the main entrance, you will find yourself in the central atrium. Directly ahead is the Exhibition Hall, our largest gallery, currently hosting the permanent collection on the region's industrial heritage. To your left, you will find the Gift Shop, where you can browse a wide selection of books, prints, and locally crafted souvenirs — a wonderful place to visit before you leave.

On your right as you face the exhibition hall is the Café, where hot and cold refreshments are available from nine in the morning until five in the afternoon. We recommend the locally sourced cream tea, which has become something of an institution among our regular visitors.

If you proceed down the corridor to the north wing, you will discover the Children's Gallery — an interactive space specifically designed for younger visitors, with hands-on displays and creative activities. Adults accompanying children are warmly welcome. At the far end of the north wing, through the double doors, is the Auditorium, which is used for our regular programme of lectures, film screenings, and community events.

A few important facts about the museum itself: we were founded in 1887 as a private collection donated to the city by a local industrialist. Today we are fully publicly funded. Admission is free for children under twelve, and concession rates are available for students and seniors. Our current temporary exhibition on the history of local textile manufacturing runs until 31st March. We would strongly encourage you to visit before it closes.
Guided tours of the main collection begin at eleven o'clock every Saturday morning, departing from the main entrance hall. Places are limited, so please register at the front desk on arrival.

Finally, please note that photography is not permitted in the Victorian gallery, where several items are on loan from national collections and subject to copyright restrictions. Photography is welcome elsewhere throughout the museum.
We hope you have a wonderful visit. Do not hesitate to ask any member of staff if you have questions.

script: Good morning everyone, and welcome to today's lecture. We'll be looking at something that most of us take entirely for granted — paper — and tracing its remarkable journey from ancient China to the digital age.

Paper was first invented in China around 105 AD, traditionally credited to a court official named Cai Lun, who worked in the imperial court of the Han Dynasty. However, archaeological evidence suggests that cruder forms of paper existed even earlier, from around the second century BC. The key material used in early Chinese papermaking was mulberry bark, which was soaked, beaten, and pressed into thin sheets. Hemp fibres and rags were also used, but mulberry was the dominant material in the classical period.

Paper-making knowledge spread westward gradually — first to Korea, then to Japan. It reached the Arab world through prisoners of war captured during the Battle of Talas in 751 AD, a pivotal conflict between Tang Dynasty China and the Abbasid Caliphate. Arab scholars and craftspeople quickly adopted and refined the technique, and for several centuries the Islamic world was the primary producer of high-quality paper in the western hemisphere.

European production of paper began in Spain in the twelfth century, introduced through the Moorish civilisation of Al-Andalus. From there, it spread gradually northward through Italy, France, and Germany. The quality of European paper improved substantially over the following centuries as new techniques were adopted and refined.

The invention of the printing press by Gutenberg around 1440 was arguably the single most transformative moment in the history of paper demand. Almost overnight, the appetite for paper expanded exponentially as books, pamphlets, and documents could be produced in quantities that were previously unimaginable.

In the modern era, paper is mainly made from wood pulp — a dramatic departure from the rag-based papers of the medieval period. Softwood trees such as spruce and pine are the primary raw materials. The environmental implications of this are significant, and the industry has faced considerable pressure to adopt more sustainable practices.

On that note — recycled paper reduces water use in the manufacturing process by up to 60 percent compared to virgin paper production, which is a considerable saving given the enormous quantities of water involved in traditional papermaking.
Today, the largest paper-producing country in the world is China, which accounts for approximately a quarter of global production, followed by the United States and Japan.

As we all know, digital documents have reduced office paper use significantly over the past two decades. However, the much-predicted "paperless office" has not fully materialised — global paper consumption has actually remained surprisingly resilient, particularly in developing economies.

Finally, looking ahead — researchers are now developing paper made from agricultural waste — materials such as sugarcane fibre and wheat straw — which may offer a genuinely sustainable alternative to wood-based paper in the coming decades. I find this one of the more exciting material science developments in a field that has been relatively stable for centuries.

L.p: Listen to a university lecture on the invention and spread of paper-making.

script: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome aboard the Greenfield Heritage Bus Tour. I'm your guide, and over the next ninety minutes we'll be taking you past the city's most significant landmarks. Please sit back, enjoy the ride, and feel free to ask questions at the end of the tour.

We're currently passing through the heart of the historic quarter. On your left you can see the magnificent City Hall. This imposing neoclassical building was constructed in 1872 and has served as the seat of local government ever since. Notice the carved stone columns and the distinctive copper dome, which has turned that beautiful shade of green over the decades due to natural oxidation. The hall is still in active use and is not open to general visitors, though it is used for official civic ceremonies throughout the year.

As we round the corner, you can see ahead of us the famous River Bridge. This elegant wrought-iron structure was originally built in the late Victorian era, but required substantial renovation as recently as 2003 after engineering surveys identified concerns with the supporting foundations. The renovation was sympathetically done and the bridge retains all its original character.

The Main Market, which you'll see on your right, operates on weekdays only — Monday to Friday — and has been a fixture of city life for over two hundred years. It specialises in fresh produce, artisan foods, and handcrafted goods, and is enormously popular with locals and tourists alike.

And now, if you look to your left, you'll see the entrance to the Botanical Garden. This remarkable green space covers 35 hectares and contains over twelve thousand plant species from around the world. It was established in the nineteenth century and is free to enter on Sundays — a fact that makes it extremely busy on weekend afternoons, so we'd recommend a midweek visit for a more peaceful experience.

script: Good morning. Today we continue our series on marine biology with a focus on one of the planet's most extraordinary and endangered ecosystems — coral reefs.

Let me begin with some context. Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they support around twenty-five percent of all marine species. That staggering disproportion tells you everything about their ecological importance — they are arguably the most productive ecosystems on Earth relative to their area.

The main threat facing reefs globally is bleaching — a process caused by rising sea temperatures. When water temperatures rise even slightly above the normal range — often by just one to two degrees Celsius — the symbiotic algae that live inside coral tissues and provide them with nutrition are expelled. Without these algae, the coral turns white — hence "bleaching" — and if the stress continues, the coral will die. This process is known as coral bleaching and has devastated reef systems worldwide, most notably the Great Barrier Reef, which has experienced multiple mass bleaching events in recent years.

Other major threats include destructive fishing practices — the use of dynamite and cyanide to catch fish — and coastal development, which generates sediment runoff that smothers reefs and reduces water clarity. Pollution from agricultural runoff also contributes significantly.

Scientists use satellite monitoring to track reef health at a global scale — this has transformed our ability to detect early warning signs of stress and respond more rapidly. At a more granular level, underwater surveys and temperature sensors provide detailed data on specific reef systems.

In terms of restoration, the two most promising methods currently in use are coral transplanting — growing coral fragments in nurseries and attaching them to damaged reefs — and the use of artificial structures, such as specially designed reef modules, which provide new substrate for coral larvae to settle on.

The economic dimension is also significant. The Great Barrier Reef alone generates approximately 6 billion dollars annually for the Australian economy through tourism, fishing, and related industries — making reef conservation not merely an environmental imperative but an economic one.

Finally, international conservation efforts are coordinated under frameworks such as the Biodiversity Convention, which provides the legal and policy architecture for national governments to develop and implement reef protection strategies.

And joining me now is Sarah Greer from the Millfield Community Garden Project. Sarah, can you tell us how this all began?
Sarah

Absolutely. The project actually started because of a local residents' initiative — a small group of neighbours who were tired of seeing a derelict plot of land in the middle of the estate and decided to do something constructive with it. We didn't receive any government funding at the outset, though grants have helped us since.
Presenter
And how big is the garden today?
Sarah

We currently have 36 individual growing plots — it's grown considerably from the original twelve. We had to expand into the adjacent site last year because demand completely outstripped what we had available.
Presenter
What's required to get involved?
Sarah

New members must attend a training session — that's non-negotiable. It covers everything from soil preparation to pest management to responsible use of tools. We find that members who attend are significantly more successful and much less likely to abandon their plots.
Presenter
And what does membership cost?
Sarah
The annual fee is £35. We deliberately keep it accessible. It covers your plot rental, access to communal tools and equipment, and the composting facilities.
Presenter
What's the most popular thing people grow?
Sarah

Without question, tomatoes. Every year, regardless of the weather. I think people just love the satisfaction of growing something they'll actually eat — and a homegrown tomato really does taste completely different.
Presenter
What are the opening hours?
Sarah
We're open dawn to dusk every day of the year, including bank holidays. The key code is changed monthly and sent to all current members.

script: Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture explores the psychology behind how we make decisions — a topic that sits at the intersection of cognitive science, economics, and behavioural science.

We'll start with Daniel Kahneman's dual-process theory, arguably the most influential framework in the field. Kahneman distinguishes between two modes of thinking. System 1 is fast and intuitive — it operates automatically, requires little conscious effort, and relies on mental shortcuts or "heuristics." System 2, by contrast, is slow and deliberate — it's analytical, effortful, and engaged when we face complex or unfamiliar problems.
The key insight is that most of our daily decisions are made by System 1 — often without us being aware of it. This makes us efficient, but also vulnerable to predictable errors in judgment.

One of the most well-documented biases is anchoring. When making a numerical estimate or decision, we are disproportionately influenced by the first number or figure we encounter, even if it's entirely arbitrary. Classic experiments have shown that people's salary negotiations, house price estimations, and even criminal sentencing recommendations are all affected by irrelevant initial numbers.

The availability heuristic leads us to overweight information that is recent or memorable. We judge the likelihood of events based on how easily examples come to mind — which is why vivid news stories can distort our risk perception far beyond actual statistical probabilities.

Confirmation bias is our tendency to seek and favour information that confirms our existing beliefs, while discounting contradictory evidence. This has profound implications for scientific reasoning, political discourse, and even clinical medicine.

Kahneman's research also demonstrated a powerful asymmetry: people are consistently more strongly motivated to avoid losses than to acquire equivalent gains. This is known as loss aversion, and it influences everything from financial decisions to policy compliance.

The policy applications of this work are substantial. Nudge theory, associated with Thaler and Sunstein, proposes that we can improve decision-making by redesigning the choice or decision architecture — the environment in which decisions are made — without removing freedom of choice. Governments have applied nudges to encourage financial saving, pension enrolment, and organ donation, achieving significant behavioural change at minimal cost.

Critics argue, however, that nudges undermine individual autonomy by manipulating rather than informing. Looking ahead, researchers are increasingly focused on the role of artificial intelligence and digital platforms in shaping decision environments — a frontier with enormous ethical implications.

script: Good afternoon, everyone. Today's lecture examines one of the most extraordinary commercial and cultural systems in human history — the Silk Road.

Firstly, I want to dispel a common misconception. The Silk Road was not a single road. It was a network of overland and maritime trade routes connecting East Asia to the Mediterranean world — a vast, sprawling web of paths, caravan tracks, and sea lanes that evolved over many centuries.

This network connected China to the Mediterranean, passing through Central Asia, Persia, and the Levant. At its height, goods could travel from Chang'an — modern-day Xi'an — all the way to Rome or Alexandria, changing hands many times along the way.

The name comes, of course, from silk — a luxury product that only China knew how to produce for much of antiquity and which commanded extraordinary prices in western markets. But silk was only one of many commodities exchanged. Spices, glassware, paper, precious metals, and textiles also moved along these routes, alongside ideas, technologies, and religions.

The city of Samarkand in present-day Uzbekistan was perhaps the greatest hub of Silk Road commerce — positioned at the intersection of multiple routes, it grew fabulously wealthy as a centre of trade and culture.

The Silk Road was also a highway for belief systems. Buddhism spread westward from India, while Christianity and Islam spread eastward through contact along these routes. This cultural exchange was arguably as significant as any commercial transaction.
The routes also carried pestilence. Historians believe the Black Death, which devastated Eurasia in the fourteenth century, may have spread via overland trade routes from Central Asia.
The Silk Road's decline began in the fifteenth century with the rise of maritime trade — European sailors found sea routes to Asia that were faster and cheaper than overland caravans.

Today, China's Belt and Road Initiative is often described as a modern reinvention of the Silk Road concept — a vast infrastructure investment programme aimed at connecting Asia, Africa, and Europe through trade corridors.

script: Good morning. Today's lecture covers the foundational theories of cognitive development — specifically the work of Piaget and Vygotsky, and what modern neuroscience adds to their frameworks.

Jean Piaget proposed that children move through four sequential stages of cognitive development. The first is the sensorimotor stage, covering birth to age two. The second is the preoperational stage, from two to seven. Third comes the Concrete Operational stage — ages seven to eleven — during which children develop logical thinking about concrete objects. Finally, from about twelve onwards, the formal operational stage emerges, characterised by abstract reasoning.

Object permanence — the understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight — develops during the sensorimotor stage, typically around eight to twelve months. Before this, infants act as though objects that disappear simply cease to exist.
The language explosion — that dramatic acceleration in vocabulary acquisition — typically occurs between 18 months and 3 years. In this period, children may learn several new words every single day.

Vygotsky's contribution centred on the social dimension of learning. He introduced the concept of the Zone of Proximal Development — defined as the gap between what a child can achieve independently and what they can achieve with guidance from a more capable peer or adult.

Scaffolding refers to the structured support provided by a more capable peer or adult — it's the practical application of the ZPD concept. As the child becomes more competent, the scaffold is gradually withdrawn.
Attachment theory was developed by Bowlby in the mid-twentieth century. His research showed that secure early attachment is strongly predictive of better academic and social outcomes later in life.

Modern research uses brain and neurological imaging — techniques like fMRI — to study how cognitive development unfolds at a neural level. This has confirmed and refined many of Piaget and Vygotsky's insights.

And finally, early childhood intervention programmes — like Sure Start in the UK — have been shown to significantly reduce educational inequality by supporting development in the critical early years.

script: Good morning. Today we turn to one of the most significant demographic shifts in human history — the rapid urbanisation of the world's population.
By 2050, it is projected that approximately 68% of the world's population will live in urban areas, up from around 55% today. This represents a transformation without historical precedent.

The largest urban migration currently underway is in China and India, where hundreds of millions of people have moved from rural areas to cities in the span of just two or three generations. The speed and scale of this transition is extraordinary.

Rapid urbanisation without adequate planning leads to informal settlements — known in different contexts as slums or favelas — where millions live without access to clean water, sanitation, or legal housing tenure.
The United Nations programme addressing urban poverty and sustainable city development is called UN-Habitat, which works with national governments and cities to improve planning frameworks.
Smart city technology — sensors, data analytics, intelligent transport — can reduce urban energy use by up to 30%, which has significant implications for climate targets.

script: Good morning, everyone. Today we're exploring one of the fastest-growing fields in biomedical science — the human microbiome.

The human body contains approximately 37 trillion microbial cells — comparable in number to the body's own cells. The vast majority of these microbes reside in the gut, particularly the large intestine.

The gut microbiome consists of an astonishing variety of bacteria — estimates suggest between 500 and 1000 distinct bacterial species in a typical healthy adult gut, though this varies considerably between individuals based on diet, environment, and genetics.

What do these bacteria do? Their functions are remarkably varied. They assist with digestion — breaking down complex carbohydrates and fibre that our own enzymes can't process. They play a crucial role in immune system regulation and support — approximately 70% of the immune system resides in the gut. And they synthesise vitamins, including vitamin K and several B vitamins.

When the normal balance of the microbiome is disrupted — by illness, antibiotic use, or poor diet — the resulting condition is called dysbiosis. This imbalance has been associated with a wide range of health conditions.
Antibiotics, while life-saving, can reduce microbiome diversity by up to 90% — and in some cases, the microbiome may take months or years to fully recover.
Probiotics are live and beneficial bacteria — found in fermented foods like yoghurt, kefir, and sauerkraut — that can help restore microbial balance.
Prebiotics, by contrast, are dietary fibre components that specifically feed beneficial gut bacteria, promoting their growth and activity.

The gut-brain axis is a fascinating bidirectional communication system linking the microbiome to mental and brain health. Emerging research suggests the microbiome influences mood, cognition, and even risk of depression and anxiety.

We're increasingly linking microbiome imbalance to inflammation, obesity, and a growing list of chronic conditions. This is why personalised microbiome medicine is considered one of the most promising frontiers in 21st-century healthcare.

script: Good morning. Today we're examining the history of photography — from its invention in the nineteenth century to the AI-assisted image-making of today.

The first permanent photograph was taken in 1826 or 1827 — historians debate the exact year — by a French inventor. That inventor was Joseph Nicéphore Niépce, who captured a view from his window using a pewter plate coated with bitumen. The exposure took approximately eight hours.

The daguerreotype — a more practical and widely reproducible photographic process — was introduced in 1839 and rapidly became popular across Europe and North America. It's often considered the true birth of photography as a practical medium.

Film-based photography dominated the industry from the 1880s to the 1990s, when digital technology began to supplant it. The photographic film industry was enormously profitable during this period, with Kodak alone at its peak controlling a significant share of global consumer photography.
The first digital camera was developed by a Kodak engineer called Steven Sasson in 1975 — a prototype that weighed 3.6 kilograms and captured an image with a resolution of 0.01 megapixels.
Digital photography went mainstream in the 2000s, as prices dropped and quality improved rapidly. Within a decade, film cameras had become largely obsolete for most consumers.

Today, smartphone cameras account for over 92% of all photographs taken globally. The quality of mobile phone cameras has advanced to the point where they rival — and in some contexts surpass — traditional dedicated cameras.
Artificial intelligence now assists with autofocus and composition — and increasingly with post-processing, noise reduction, and scene recognition.
Photography was first recognised as a serious art form in the 20th century, when galleries and museums began to accept photographs alongside paintings and sculpture.
Current debates in photography ethics focus on issues of privacy and authenticity — particularly in the age of AI image generation and sophisticated manipulation software.

script: Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture examines one of the most rapidly developing applications of artificial intelligence — its use in healthcare.

AI systems are now capable of analysing medical images — X-rays, MRI scans, retinal photographs — with remarkable accuracy. In some benchmarked studies, AI image analysis has achieved 94% accuracy in detecting certain conditions, comparable to or exceeding experienced radiologists.

AI cannot replace the clinical and human judgement of a doctor — the contextual, relational, and ethical dimensions of medicine require human intelligence.

script: Good morning. Today we conclude our series on cognitive science with a deep dive into the neuroscience of memory — how we form, store, and retrieve information, and what happens when these processes break down.

Memory is broadly divided into short-term or working memory and long-term memory. Working memory is the system that temporarily holds information in conscious awareness for active processing — it's what you use when you're mentally performing arithmetic or holding a phone number in mind.

The capacity of working memory is famously limited. Cognitive psychologist George Miller described it as seven, plus or minus two — meaning most people can hold between five and nine items at once in working memory. More recent research suggests the true figure may be closer to four items.

The hippocampus — a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the medial temporal lobe — plays a central role in encoding or forming new memories. It acts as a binding agent, integrating information from different sensory systems into a coherent episodic memory.

Damage to the hippocampus causes anterograde amnesia — the inability to form new long-term memories. The patient can remember everything from before the damage, but cannot create new memories after it. The famous case of H.M. — who underwent bilateral hippocampal removal in 1953 — remains the most studied case in neuropsychological history.
Long-term memory is divided into explicit or declarative memory — which includes episodic and semantic memory — and implicit memory, which covers skills and conditioned responses.
Procedural memory — how to ride a bicycle, how to play a musical instrument — is stored primarily in the basal ganglia and cerebellum, explaining why these skills survive hippocampal damage.
Sleep is critical for memory consolidation. Memories are replayed and stabilised during REM and deep sleep, which is why sleep deprivation has such dramatic effects on learning and recall.
The "spacing effect" refers to the well-established finding that spaced study — distributing study sessions over time — produces far better long-term retention than massed or cramming.
Stress has complex effects on memory. The hormone cortisol, released during stress, enhances memory formation for emotionally significant events but can impair the formation of neutral memories.
Finally, promising treatments for memory disorders include transcranial magnetic and deep brain stimulation techniques, which are being trialled for conditions including Alzheimer's disease.

text: **A** Today salt is so cheap that most of us hardly think about it, yet for most of human history it was one of the most valuable substances on Earth. The reason is simple: before refrigeration, salt was the main way of stopping food from going bad. Meat and fish packed in salt could be kept for months, which allowed people to store food for the winter and to carry it on long journeys.

**B** Archaeologists have found evidence that people were producing salt at least 8,000 years ago. One of the oldest known sites is in present-day Romania, where early farmers boiled the water of salty springs until only the crystals remained. In China, too, salt was gathered from the shores of salt lakes in prehistoric times.

**C** Because salt was so useful, it became a source of wealth and power. Roads were built to carry it: the Via Salaria, one of the oldest roads in Italy, takes its name from the salt that was transported along it to Rome. The English word 'salary' comes from the Latin salarium, which is related to sal, the Latin word for salt. However, historians now doubt the popular story that Roman soldiers were actually paid in salt.

**D** Governments soon realised that salt could be taxed, since everyone needed it. In France, a hated salt tax known as the gabelle was one of the grievances that contributed to the French Revolution. In British-ruled India, a law that made it illegal for Indians to produce their own salt led to Gandhi's famous Salt March in 1930, when thousands of people walked to the sea to make salt in protest.

**E** Today the situation is very different. Only a small proportion of the salt produced worldwide ends up in food. Most is used by industry, particularly in the manufacture of chemicals such as chlorine, and large amounts are spread on roads in winter to stop ice from forming.

**F** Ironically, in many countries the main health concern about salt is no longer scarcity but excess. Doctors warn that eating too much salt raises blood pressure, and some governments now encourage food manufacturers to reduce the salt they add to bread, soups and ready meals.

text: **A** Bees do far more than make honey. As they move from flower to flower collecting nectar, they carry pollen between plants, allowing them to produce seeds and fruit. Around three-quarters of the world's main food crops benefit to some degree from animal pollination, and bees are the most important pollinators of all.

**B** Since the 1990s, beekeepers in Europe and North America have reported unusually heavy losses of honeybee colonies. In 2006, American beekeepers began describing a mysterious condition in which most of the adult bees in a hive simply disappeared, leaving the queen and the young behind. It became known as colony collapse disorder.

**C** Scientists now believe that there is no single cause. Instead, several pressures act together. A parasitic mite called Varroa feeds on bees and spreads viruses between them. Certain pesticides, especially a group known as neonicotinoids, can affect bees' ability to navigate and find their way back to the hive. And the loss of wildflower meadows means that bees have fewer and less varied sources of food, which weakens their resistance to disease.

**D** Wild bees face similar threats, and they are often harder to protect because nobody looks after them. Britain alone has around 270 species of bee, and most of them are solitary: rather than living in colonies, each female builds her own small nest.

**E** There are encouraging signs. In 2018 the European Union banned the outdoor use of three neonicotinoid pesticides. Farmers are being paid to leave strips of wildflowers along the edges of their fields, and many towns now leave road verges uncut until late summer so that flowers can bloom.

**F** Individuals can help too. Planting a variety of flowers that bloom at different times of year gives bees food from spring to autumn, and leaving a corner of the garden untidy provides nesting places for wild bees.

text: **A** Rewilding is an approach to conservation that aims to restore natural processes rather than manage nature in detail. Instead of deciding exactly which plants should grow where, rewilders try to bring back missing species and then step back, allowing ecosystems to recover in their own way.

**B** The best-known example comes from Yellowstone National Park in the United States, where grey wolves were reintroduced in 1995 after an absence of about seventy years. The wolves reduced the number of elk and changed where the elk grazed. Some scientists argue that this allowed willow and aspen trees to grow back along rivers, although the size of this effect is still debated.

**C** In Britain, one of the most talked-about projects is the Knepp estate in West Sussex. In 2001 its owners decided that farming its heavy clay soil was no longer profitable, so they let the land go wild. Free-roaming cattle, pigs, ponies and deer now graze the land, and rare species such as nightingales and purple emperor butterflies have returned in growing numbers.

**D** Beavers have also become symbols of rewilding. Hunted to extinction in Britain centuries ago, they are now back in a number of rivers. By building dams, they create ponds and wetlands that hold back water during heavy rain, which can reduce flooding further downstream.

**E** Rewilding has its critics. Some farmers worry that land taken out of production will reduce the amount of food the country grows, and sheep farmers in particular fear that the return of predators such as the lynx would put their animals at risk. Others point out that a landscape left to itself does not always become richer in wildlife.

**F** Supporters reply that rewilding does not have to mean huge areas or dangerous predators. Even small projects – a river allowed to follow its natural course, or a field left to become woodland – can make a measurable difference.

text: **A** Everyone sleeps, yet scientists are still discovering exactly why. We spend roughly a third of our lives asleep, and going without sleep for long periods damages both the body and the mind. Adults generally need between seven and nine hours a night, while teenagers need more.

**B** Sleep is not a single state. During the night we pass through several cycles, each lasting about ninety minutes. Each cycle includes light sleep, deep sleep and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, when the eyes move quickly beneath the eyelids and most vivid dreaming takes place.

**C** Deep sleep appears to be especially important for the body. During this stage the body repairs tissues and releases growth hormone, and the immune system is strengthened. REM sleep, on the other hand, seems to play a central role in processing emotions and memories.

**D** One of the most striking recent discoveries concerns the brain's cleaning system. In 2013, researchers working with mice found that during sleep the spaces between brain cells widen, allowing fluid to wash away waste products that build up during the day. If the same happens in humans, it may help to explain why poor sleep has been linked to a higher risk of dementia.

**E** Our sleep is controlled partly by an internal body clock, which follows a cycle of roughly 24 hours. Light is the most powerful signal for this clock. Bright light in the evening – including light from phone and computer screens – can delay the release of melatonin, a hormone that makes us feel sleepy, so that we fall asleep later.
**F** Sleep experts recommend a few simple habits: going to bed and getting up at the same time every day, keeping the bedroom cool and dark, and avoiding caffeine in the afternoon and evening.

text: **A** Almost everyone puts things off from time to time, but for some people procrastination is a serious problem that affects their studies, their work and even their health. Surveys suggest that around one in five adults describe themselves as chronic procrastinators.

**B** For a long time, procrastination was seen as a problem of time management: people delayed tasks because they were disorganised or lazy. Psychologists now see it differently. Many researchers describe procrastination as a problem of managing emotions rather than time. When a task makes us feel anxious, bored or insecure, putting it off brings immediate relief – even though the task, and the bad feeling, will still be there tomorrow.

**C** This helps to explain why procrastinators are often perfectionists. If you are afraid that your work will not be good enough, starting it means facing that fear. Delaying the task protects you from it, at least for a while.

**D** Procrastination also reflects the way the brain values rewards. We tend to give more weight to rewards that come immediately than to those that come later. Checking a phone brings an instant reward, while the benefits of finishing an essay may be weeks away.

Some people use a 'five-minute rule': they agree to work on a task for just five minutes, knowing that they can stop afterwards – and often find that they carry on. text: **A** Writing is one of humanity's most important inventions, yet for most of our history people managed without it. The earliest known writing appeared in Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, a little over 5,000 years ago.

text: **A** For most of history, infectious diseases were the greatest threat to human life. Smallpox alone killed hundreds of millions of people in the twentieth century before it was finally wiped out.

**B** Long before vaccines, people in China, India and parts of Africa and the Middle East practised variolation: material from the sores of someone with a mild case of smallpox was deliberately introduced into a healthy person, usually through a small cut. Most people treated in this way developed a mild illness and were then protected, although some became seriously ill.

**C** In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner tested an idea that was already known among country people: that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease of cattle, did not catch smallpox. He took material from a cowpox sore on a milkmaid's hand and introduced it into a boy called James Phipps. When Jenner later exposed the boy to smallpox, he did not fall ill.

**D** The word 'vaccine' comes from vacca, the Latin word for cow, in honour of Jenner's work. Almost a century later, Louis Pasteur took the idea further, developing vaccines against chicken cholera, anthrax and rabies in his laboratory.

**E** The twentieth century brought vaccines against diphtheria, tetanus, polio, measles and many other diseases. In 1980, after a worldwide vaccination campaign led by the World Health Organization, smallpox became the first human disease to be completely eradicated.

In my view, while serious and violent offences undoubtedly warrant custodial sentences, society's ultimate goal should be the reduction of crime rather than punishment for its own sake. model.p: In an era characterised by perpetual connectivity and intensifying professional demands, the erosion of the boundary between working life and personal time has become one of the most pervasive challenges facing working adults across the world. The consequences of chronic work-life imbalance are serious and wide-ranging, affecting individuals, families, and organisations alike.

At the individual level, the most immediate consequence is the deterioration of physical and mental health. Prolonged overwork is strongly associated with burnout, anxiety, depression, cardiovascular disease, and disrupted sleep. Relationships also suffer significantly when one partner consistently prioritises professional obligations over family commitments, leading to marital breakdown, strained parent-child bonds, and social isolation. These personal consequences carry substantial economic costs: reduced productivity, increased absenteeism, and higher staff turnover impose enormous financial burdens on businesses, while the wider healthcare and social costs are borne by governments and communities.

Addressing this issue requires intervention at both the organisational and policy levels. Employers have a direct responsibility — and, increasingly, a legal obligation in many jurisdictions — to prevent excessive working hours and to create cultures in which taking leave is actively encouraged rather than implicitly discouraged. Implementing flexible working arrangements, including remote work and variable hours, has been shown to improve both employee wellbeing and productivity. Technology companies, meanwhile, should develop tools that allow employees to set and enforce boundaries on after-hours communication.

At the governmental level, stronger enforcement of existing working time regulations is essential, along with the introduction of enhanced parental leave provisions and affordable childcare, which disproportionately affects working parents, particularly women. Public awareness campaigns that challenge the cultural glorification of overwork would also contribute to a meaningful shift in societal attitudes.

In conclusion, work-life balance is not a luxury but a prerequisite for individual wellbeing and sustained organisational performance. Achieving it requires systemic change rather than individual willpower alone.

model.p: The proposal that governments should mandate regular medical check-ups for all citizens is motivated by a genuine and laudable concern for public health. However, I believe that making such check-ups compulsory would be disproportionate and raises significant ethical concerns, even though preventative healthcare is undeniably important.

The strongest argument in favour of compulsory check-ups is that many serious conditions — including hypertension, diabetes, and certain cancers — are asymptomatic in their early stages and are therefore frequently undiagnosed until they have progressed to a point where treatment is both more complex and more costly. By identifying such conditions early, regular screening could save lives and reduce the long-term financial burden on public health systems. Governments already require various forms of compulsory health measures, such as childhood vaccinations, and a similar rationale could be applied here.

Nevertheless, I strongly believe that compulsion is the wrong approach. Forcing adults to undergo medical examinations against their will represents a serious intrusion on bodily autonomy and personal liberty — values that are fundamental to any democratic society. Furthermore, the enforcement of such a policy would be logistically extremely challenging and would risk disproportionately penalising vulnerable groups, such as those living in poverty or in rural areas with limited access to healthcare. The financial costs of implementation would also be enormous.

A far more effective strategy would be to invest heavily in public education campaigns that highlight the benefits of preventative healthcare, to remove financial barriers by ensuring that check-ups are freely available, and to incentivise participation through positive means — such as reduced health insurance premiums — rather than through compulsion. Encouraging healthy behaviour through education and accessibility is both more respectful and, evidence suggests, more effective in the long run.

model.p: The decision of whether to take a gap year between school and university is one that divides opinion sharply. I firmly believe, however, that a well-planned gap year can be an enormously valuable experience, and the characterisation of it as a waste of time is both reductive and largely inaccurate.

Critics of gap years often argue that students who take a year out lose academic momentum, allow knowledge acquired during school to fade, and may struggle to re-engage with formal study upon returning. There is a further concern that, for some students, a gap year becomes an indefinite period of aimless deferral rather than purposeful development.

These concerns, while not entirely without merit, overlook the profound benefits that a well-structured gap year provides. Students who spend this period working, volunteering, or travelling abroad return to university with a significantly enhanced sense of self-awareness, clearer academic and career goals, and a greater appreciation for the value of higher education. Research from several UK and Australian universities indicates that gap year students consistently outperform their peers academically in their first year and are considerably less likely to drop out. This may be because they have chosen their degree programme with greater deliberation and are intrinsically more motivated as a result.

Furthermore, the experiences gained during a gap year — whether developing professional skills in a workplace, acquiring a second language abroad, or building resilience through independent travel — represent a form of personal education that no classroom curriculum can fully replicate. These qualities are highly valued by graduate employers and contribute to the development of well-rounded, adaptable individuals.

In conclusion, provided it is approached with intention and used productively, a gap year is not merely acceptable but actively beneficial. The risk of wasting time is real, but it is one that responsible, motivated young people are well-equipped to manage.

L.h: Linking ideas like a Band 9 writer

L.p: Linking words show how one idea relates to the next. Use them accurately and not too often: one clear linker at the start of a sentence is better than three in a row.

t: Furthermore, … / Moreover, … / In addition, … / Not only … but also …
Nevertheless, … / Conversely, … / While this may be true, …
A notable illustration of this is … / This is exemplified by …
Consequently, … / This inevitably leads to … / This can be attributed to …
Admittedly, … / It must be acknowledged that …
In conclusion, … / On balance, … / All things considered, …

L.x: *Although the plan was expensive, it* (not *Although the plan was expensive, but it*) worked.

L.tip: Don't start every sentence with a linker. Good writing also links ideas with pronouns (this, these), relative clauses and repeated key nouns.

L.p: A *cleft sentence* splits one sentence into two parts to put the focus on one element. With *It is/was … that/who …*, the part after *It is/was* is emphasised.

t: *It was John who* solved the problem.
*It is deforestation that* causes habitat loss.

L.p: *What + clause + is/was …* puts the focus at the end of the sentence. *All + clause + is/was …* means 'the only thing'.

t: I'm only saying we should act now.
*All I'm saying is* that we should act now.

L.x: *What we need is* (not *What we need are*) a clear plan.

L.tip: Clefts are excellent in Speaking Part 3 for stressing your main point: *What really worries me is …*

L.p: A participle clause can replace a longer clause and make writing more concise. An *-ing* clause can show two actions at the same time, or a reason.

t: Because she lacked funds, she couldn't continue.
As he walked through the city, he noticed the pollution.
*Walking through the city*, he noticed the pollution.

L.h: B Past participles and having done

L.p: A past participle has a passive meaning. *Having* + past participle shows that one action was finished before the next.

t: The policy, which was introduced in 2010, has worked.
Because they were properly trained, the staff did well.
After he had considered every option, he decided.

L.x: Having finished the report, *she sent it* (not *it was sent*) to her manager.

L.tip: The subject of the participle clause must be the same as the subject of the main clause. *Walking home, I saw a fox* – I was walking, not the fox.

L.h: A Verbs and adjectives into nouns

L.p: *Nominalisation* means using a noun where you might use a verb or an adjective. It makes writing more formal and lets you pack more information into a sentence – a key feature of academic English.

t: The *implementation* of the policy was slow.
The *significance* of the findings is clear.
Scientists discovered that CO₂ levels are rising.
The *discovery* of rising CO₂ levels alarmed scientists.
The government decided to cut subsidies.
The government's *decision* to cut subsidies was controversial.

L.x: The *development* (not *develop*) of the city centre took ten years.

L.tip: Don't overdo it: a text full of nouns is hard to read. Mix nominalised sentences with clear verbs.

L.p: *Hedging* means making a claim less absolute, so that it matches the evidence. Band 9 essays avoid overgeneralising: they say *tends to*, *may* and *suggests* rather than *always*, *will* and *proves*.

L.p: *Parallel structure* means using the same grammatical form for items joined by *and*, *or*, *but*, *both … and*, *either … or*, *neither … nor* and *not only … but also*. It makes sentences balanced and easy to follow.

t: She likes to run, swimming and to cycle.
The plan is effective, affordable and it can be done quickly.
The plan is *effective, affordable and quick*.
He was praised not only for his skill but also he worked hard.
He was praised *not only for his skill but also for his hard work*.
The policy aims to reduce costs, improving access and it created jobs.
The policy aims *to reduce costs, improve access and create jobs*.

L.x: The course is both *challenging and rewarding* (not *challenging and it rewards you*).
